title: Lower Urinary Tract Infection Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing suspected lower urinary tract infection, distinguishing uncomplicated cystitis from pyelonephritis and important alternatives, and supporting appropriate urine testing, treatment, referral and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Confirm that symptoms localise to the lower urinary tract, actively exclude pyelonephritis and sepsis, and identify factors that make the infection complicated or require culture.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Lower urinary tract infection.
Pyelonephritis or systemic urinary infection.
Sepsis or acute kidney injury.
Pregnancy.
Prostatitis in men.
Urinary retention, obstruction or significant structural urinary disease.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria or a non-urinary cause of symptoms.
Recurrent infection, catheter use or other factors requiring a different pathway.
items.importantLimitation: Positive urine dipstick or bacteriuria does not by itself establish symptomatic UTI, particularly in older adults and catheterised patients. Interpret urine findings in the clinical context.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Identify localising urinary symptoms and then screen for upper-tract, systemic and alternative causes.

items.title: Lower urinary symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: New dysuria.
Urinary frequency or urgency.
Suprapubic discomfort.
New nocturia or incontinence where clinically relevant.
Visible haematuria.

items.title: Upper-tract and systemic features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, rigors or marked systemic upset.
Flank or loin pain.
Nausea or vomiting.
Reduced urine output.
New confusion or functional deterioration in an older or frail patient.

items.title: Complicating factors
mustConfirmOrExclude: Pregnancy or possibility of pregnancy.
Male sex and symptoms of prostatitis or urinary obstruction.
Catheter or recent urinary instrumentation.
Known stones, structural urinary abnormality or recurrent UTI.
Immunosuppression, renal disease or diabetes.
Recent urine culture results and antibiotic exposure.

items.title: Alternative diagnosis features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Vaginal discharge, irritation or symptoms suggesting vulvovaginal infection.
Urethral discharge or STI risk.
Pelvic pain or pregnancy-related symptoms.
Renal colic-type pain.

sections.title: Red flags and complications
sections.intro: Do not manage as uncomplicated lower UTI when upper-tract, systemic or obstructive features are present.

items.title: Possible pyelonephritis
urgentFeatures: Fever or rigors with flank/loin pain.
Nausea or vomiting with suspected urinary infection.
implications: Use the Acute Pyelonephritis Assessment and upper-UTI treatment pathway.

items.title: Sepsis or acute kidney injury
urgentFeatures: Physiological instability, poor perfusion or altered mental state.
Markedly reduced urine output or concern for acute kidney injury.

items.title: Obstruction or retention
urgentFeatures: Inability to pass urine, painful bladder distension or significant new retention.
Suspected infected obstructed system or stone with systemic illness.
implications: Urgent urological or hospital assessment may be required.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examination should focus on systemic illness, hydration, abdominal findings and signs suggesting upper-tract or alternative pathology.

items.title: General assessment and observations
howToTest: Assess overall appearance, hydration and mental state.
Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and other observations where clinically indicated.
normal: Clinically well, hydrated and physiologically stable.
abnormal: Fever, hypotension, tachycardia, dehydration or altered mental state.
implications: Systemic abnormalities raise concern for upper-tract infection or another acute illness.

items.title: Abdominal and renal examination
howToTest: Assess for flank or costovertebral-angle tenderness.
Look for abdominal distension or a palpable bladder when retention is suspected.
normal: No significant flank tenderness, peritonism or bladder distension.
abnormal: Flank/CVA tenderness, peritonism or evidence of retention.
implications: Flank tenderness with systemic features supports pyelonephritis; retention or peritonism requires an alternative pathway.

sections.title: Urine testing and investigations
sections.intro: Testing strategy depends on age, sex, pregnancy, catheter status, recurrence and illness severity.

items.title: Urine testing
mustConfirmOrExclude: Use urine dipstick only in patient groups where it is clinically appropriate; do not use it as a stand-alone diagnosis.
Obtain urine culture when required by the relevant pathway, including pregnancy, men, recurrent or complicated infection, treatment failure and suspected pyelonephritis.
Obtain a urine sample before antibiotics when this is required and does not delay urgent treatment.
Review previous culture and susceptibility results where available.

items.title: Additional investigations
mustConfirmOrExclude: Consider renal function, blood tests or imaging when systemic illness, AKI, obstruction, stone or another complication is suspected.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Treatment should reflect patient group, complication risk and previous microbiology rather than a single generic UTI pathway.

items.title: Treatment
mustConfirmOrExclude: Use the appropriate lower-UTI prescribing pathway for the patient's sex and pregnancy status.
Take previous urine culture and antibiotic exposure into account.
Provide hydration, symptom-control and follow-up advice.

items.title: Community management may be appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No pyelonephritis, sepsis, AKI or obstructive red flag is present.
The patient can maintain oral fluids and treatment.
Complicating factors have been addressed and appropriate urine testing arranged.
Reliable reassessment is available.

sections.title: Safety-netting
sections.intro: Advise prompt reassessment if symptoms evolve towards upper-tract or systemic infection.

items.title: Advise urgent reassessment if
safetyNetting: Fever, rigors, flank pain, vomiting or marked systemic illness develops.
Symptoms worsen rapidly or fail to improve after treatment starts.
The patient becomes unable to maintain fluids or oral medication.
New retention or severe pain develops.
